item.mechanism: Severe local lattice distortion caused by the presence of many elements with different atomic sizes impedes dislocation motion, leading to pronounced strengthening.
item.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) with ≥5 principal components
item.operating_conditions: General condition for HEAs; implied room temperature and elevated temperatures where dislocation motion is the primary deformation mode
item.supporting_observation: The text states that atoms in HEAs tend to deviate from ideal lattice sites due to atomic size differences, which impedes dislocation motion.
item.scope_limits: The text notes this is a general concept for HEAs but does not quantify the specific contribution in the Al-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ti system compared to other mechanisms like precipitation strengthening.
item.alternatives_considered: Traditional alloy design using one or two key components; formation of brittle intermetallic phases like C14 Laves phase.
quotes: Due to the existence of many kinds of elements with different atomic sizes, atoms in HEAs tend to deviate from their ideal lattice sites and give rise to severe local lattice distortion
which could impede dislocation motion, leading to the pronounced strengthening effect
using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components

item.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening occurs via coherent nanoscale L2 1 precipitates in a BCC matrix, where the hard L2 1 phase bears a larger load (load transfer) upon yielding of the soft BCC matrix.
item.system: Alloy 1 (Al 20 Cr 5 Fe 50 Mn 20 Ti 5) and Alloy 8 (Al 15 Cr 5 Fe 50 Mn 25 Ti 5)
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures up to 700 °C; as-cast state and after homogenization at 1200 °C
item.supporting_observation: In situ neutron diffraction showed clear load-transfer behavior in Alloy 1, where the L2 1 phase exhibited greater lattice strains than the BCC phase upon yielding.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for Alloys 2–7 (Group 2), which exhibit an L2 1 antiphase domain (APD) morphology behaving like a single phase with no load transfer.
item.alternatives_considered: Intrinsic deformation of a single L2 1 phase (observed in Alloys 2–7); ordering strengthening alone without load transfer.
quotes: Alloy 1 displays a clear load-transfer behavior upon the BCC phase yielding (around 1000 MPa), i.e., the hard L2 1 phase bears a larger load with greater lattice strains
while the soft BCC phase undertakes a lower load with lower lattice strains
In contrast, no load transfer was observed in Alloy 7

item.mechanism: The formation of nanoscale L2 1 precipitates within a BCC matrix is driven by chemical compositions that deviate significantly from the perfect L2 1 stoichiometry, preventing the formation of a single-phase L2 1 structure.
item.system: Alloys 1 and 8 (Group 1) in the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system
item.operating_conditions: As-cast state; solidification and cooling from molten state to room temperature
item.supporting_observation: The authors link the deviation from stoichiometry to the formation of precipitates, contrasting it with Alloys 2–7 which match stoichiometry and form APDs.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to Alloys 2–7 where compositions match the perfect L2 1 stoichiometry, resulting in a single-phase L2 1 morphology.
item.alternatives_considered: Formation of a single-phase L2 1 structure (observed in Alloys 2–7); formation of detrimental C14 Laves phase.
quotes: For G1 (Alloys 1 and 8), their chemical compositions deviate far away from the perfect L2 1 stoichiometry, leading to the formation of nanoscaled L2 1 precipitates within the BCC matrix
For G2 (Alloys 2–7), their chemical compositions can exactly match the perfect L2 1 stoichiometry, resulting in the formation of the single-phase L2 1 phase in the form of APD
The different L2 1 morphologies exhibited between G1 (nanoscale precipitates) and G2 (APDs) are strongly correlated to their different chemical compositions

item.mechanism: The stability and morphology of the L2 1 phase are governed by the order-disorder transition temperature (Tc), which is determined by the specific atomic-site occupancy and interaction energies of the constituent elements.
item.system: Alloy 1 (Al 20 Cr 5 Fe 50 Mn 20 Ti 5) and Alloy 7 (Al 30 Cr 5 Fe 50 Mn 10 Ti 5)
item.operating_conditions: Heating from room temperature to above 1000 °C; solidification and cooling processes
item.supporting_observation: Metropolis Monte Carlo (MC) calculations predicted a lower Tc for Alloy 1 (1607 °C) compared to Alloy 7 (1997 °C), consistent with experimental neutron scattering showing L2 1 stability up to 900 °C for Alloy 1 and 1050 °C for Alloy 7.
item.scope_limits: The model assumes a BCC lattice and nearest-neighbor interactions; it may not fully capture lattice distortion or vibration effects.
item.alternatives_considered: Random distribution of atoms; formation of other intermetallic phases like C14 Laves.
quotes: The ordering transition temperature, T c , of Alloy 1 [1607 °C (1880 K)] is much lower than that of Alloy 7 [1997 °C (2270 K), far beyond its melting temperature]

This prediction is consistent with the experimental observations (Fig. 4 a, b ), i.e., Alloy 1 is composed of L2 1 and BCC phases from RT to 900 °C, while only the ordered L2 1 phase still exists in Alloy 7 from RT to 1050 °C
The order-disorder transition can be directly reflected by the LRO parameters

item.mechanism: Strong interatomic pair interactions (specifically Al–Fe and Cr–Fe) promote the formation of L2 1 and BCC phases respectively, influencing the chemical segregation and phase stability.
item.operating_conditions: Molten state at 1600 °C; solid state formation
item.supporting_observation: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations showed the highest intensity for Al–Fe and Cr–Fe pair correlations in the liquid state, suggesting these interactions drive phase formation.
item.scope_limits: Based on simulations of the liquid state; the text notes that the reliability is verified by fitting neutron-scattering PDF results.
item.alternatives_considered: Random bonding; formation of other phases not driven by these specific pairs.
quotes: The persistent presence of stronger Al–Fe and Cr–Fe pair correlations in the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti alloys suggests that Al–Fe and Cr–Fe pair interactions may promote the formation of L2 1 and BCC phases, respectively

The intensities of pair correlations of the Al–Al and Ti–Ti bonds are significantly lower than the other pair correlations, indicating the strong tendency for Al and Ti atoms to bond with other elements
On the other hand, the Al–Fe pair correlation has the highest intensity, and the Cr–Fe pair correlation has the second-highest intensity

item.mechanism: Ordering strengthening contributes significantly to the yield strength, calculated to be ~904 MPa in Alloy 1, which accounts for the difference in yield strength between precipitate-strengthened alloys and those with APD morphology.
item.supporting_observation: The calculated ordering strengthening (~904 MPa) closely matches the yield strength difference between Alloy 1 and Alloys 2/7 (~874 MPa and ~860 MPa respectively).
item.scope_limits: Specific to the precipitation-strengthened morphology (Group 1); not the primary mechanism for Group 2 alloys which behave as single phases.
item.alternatives_considered: Load transfer mechanism; intrinsic deformation of L2 1 phase.
quotes: The precipitation-strengthening contribution in Alloy 1 is quantitatively calculated (Supplementary Note 1), which is mainly attributed to the ordering strengthening (~904 MPa)
close to the yield strength differences between Alloys 1 and 2 (~874 MPa), and between Alloys 1 and 7 (~860 MPa)
Therefore, the high yield strengths of Alloys 1 and 8 are attributed to the precipitation strengthening, besides the effect of atomic-level complexity in HEAs

item.mechanism: The CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method can efficiently screen thousands of compositions to identify alloys with specific phase fractions (BCC and L2 1) and melting temperatures suitable for high-temperature applications.
item.operating_conditions: Computational screening at various temperatures (Tm, 0.8Tm, 0.5Tm); step size of 5 at.%
item.supporting_observation: The method screened 3246 alloys, identifying 8 candidates that met criteria for Tm > 1250 °C and specific L2 1 volume fractions at operating temperatures.
item.scope_limits: Valid in the composition range of Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.% with unchanged contents of other elements; accuracy depends on the thermodynamic database.
item.alternatives_considered: Trial-and-error experimental method; conventional CALPHAD calculations without high-throughput automation.
quotes: Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions
Using a step size of 5 atomic percent (at.%) for each component in the composition range from 0 to 50 at.%, the solidification HTCs for a total of 3246 alloys are calculated
Only eight alloys (density, ρ ≤ 6.5 g/cm 3 ) survive out of the over 3000 compositions eventually

item.mechanism: The formation of detrimental C14 Laves phase in Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti HEAs is caused by the dissimilarity of crystal structures and different thermal expansion coefficients between the C14 Laves and BCC-base phases, increasing the tendency to crack.
item.system: Previous Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti HEAs (prior to the current study's design)
item.operating_conditions: General application conditions; implied high-temperature usage
item.supporting_observation: The authors state that the formation of this phase deteriorates properties due to structural and thermal mismatch.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism explains why previous alloys failed; the current study aims to avoid this by selecting compositions without this phase.
item.alternatives_considered: Formation of L2 1 precipitates; formation of BCC matrix.
quotes: Our previous work discovered potential L2 1 precipitation-strengthened lightweight HEAs (LWHEAs) in an Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system, but the formation of the brittle C14 Laves phase deteriorates their properties
because the dissimilarity of crystal structures and different thermal expansion coefficients between the C14 Laves and BCC-base phases increase the tendency to crack
Hence, exploring suitable chemical compositions without the formation of detrimental intermetallic phases is crucial for developing the desired materials
